theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is yeast?
options: A tiny living organism, a type of fungus
A type of salt that makes the dough rise up
A chemical powder like baking powder
A flour made from dried sugar cane

questions.stem: Which four things does yeast need to grow and make gas?
options: Salt, cold, light and dry air
Food, warmth, moisture and time
Ice, fat, darkness and no air
Heat over 80 °C, salt, oil and light

questions.stem: Which gas does yeast give off that makes dough rise?
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Nitrogen

questions.stem: Why must the liquid for a yeast dough be only lukewarm, not hot?
options: Too much heat kills the yeast
Hot water makes the flour too white
Warm liquid makes the salt work better
Hot liquid makes the crust too soft

questions.stem: Which raising agent makes Jamaican hard dough bread rise?
options: Yeast
Baking powder
Bicarbonate of soda
Whisked egg whites

questions.stem: Why is strong (bread) flour used for most yeast doughs?
options: It has less protein, so the bread is crumbly
Its high protein forms strong, stretchy gluten
It is already mixed with the yeast and the salt
It is whiter and gives a paler crust

questions.stem: Why should salt not touch the yeast directly when you weigh out the ingredients?
options: Salt can slow down or kill the yeast
Salt makes the yeast turn into sugar
Salt and yeast together go hard as rock
Salt makes the yeast smell of fish

questions.stem: In a yeast dough, what does a small amount of sugar do?
options: It stops the yeast from working at all in the dough
It feeds the yeast and helps the crust brown
It makes the gluten stronger and chewier
It keeps the dough cold while it proves

questions.stem: Which of these is an enriched yeast dough, with butter, milk or sugar added?
options: Plain water bread
A thin pizza base
Coco bread
A plain French stick

questions.stem: Why are bread ingredients weighed carefully, including the water?
options: So the bread can be sold by the litre
Because the oven will not work otherwise
So each batch comes out the same
So you do not need to knead the dough

questions.stem: In the straight dough method, how are the ingredients mixed?
options: The yeast is fermented overnight on its own first
The flour is rubbed in with fat like pastry
The eggs and sugar are whisked to a foam first
All the ingredients are mixed together at once

questions.stem: In the sponge and dough method, what is the "sponge"?
options: A small sponge cake baked to serve with the bread
A damp cloth used to cover the dough while it rests
Part of the flour, water and yeast fermented first
The soft middle of a baked loaf

questions.stem: Why is yeast dough kneaded?
options: To melt the butter into the flour
To kill any germs in the flour
To make the dough cold and firm
To develop the gluten

questions.stem: How can you test that a dough has been kneaded enough?
options: A small piece stretches thin without tearing
The dough sticks to your hands and the table
The dough is rough and breaks apart easily
The dough has turned grey and wet

questions.stem: You are kneading dough in a mixer with a dough hook. What is the safe way to check the dough?
options: Push it down with your hand while the hook turns
Switch off and wait for the hook to stop
Lift the guard and feel it on low speed
Use a spoon to poke it while the mixer runs

questions.stem: Where should dough be left for its first proof (bulk fermentation)?
options: In the freezer, so it rises slowly
Uncovered, beside an open window with a breeze
In a hot oven at about 200 °C to speed it up
Covered, in a warm place free from draughts

questions.stem: Why is the dough covered while it proves?
options: So the surface does not dry and form a skin
So the yeast cannot get any air at all while it rests
So the dough stays as cold as possible
So nobody can see how much it has risen

questions.stem: What is "knocking back" a dough?
options: Hitting the dough hard with a rolling pin to flatten it
Pressing out the gas after the first proof
Putting the dough back in the fridge
Knocking on the oven to check the bread

questions.stem: You must make rolls of 60 g each from 1.2 kg of dough. How many rolls will you get?
Why is each piece of dough rounded (moulded) into a tight ball after it is weighed?
options: To let all of the gas escape from the dough for good
To make the roll heavier when baked
To stop the yeast from working
To give a smooth skin and an even shape

questions.stem: Many bakeries do the final proof in a prover (a proving cabinet). What does it give the dough?
options: Dry, cold air to firm the dough
Strong light to colour the crust
Direct heat to start baking it
Gentle warmth and moisture

questions.stem: How can you tell when shaped dough is ready to bake?
options: It has shrunk to half its size
A gentle finger press springs back slowly
It has a hard, dry skin on top
It smells strongly of alcohol and sour milk

questions.stem: Dough was left to prove far too long. What is likely to happen when it is baked?
options: It will be tight, small and heavy
It will be extra soft and keep for weeks
It may collapse and taste sour or yeasty
It will bake in half the normal time

questions.stem: Bread came out small and heavy, with a tight crumb. Which is a likely cause?
options: It was proved in a warm, moist place
The oven was preheated before baking
The water was too hot and killed the yeast
The dough was kneaded until smooth and stretchy

questions.stem: Plain bread rolls are baked in a hot oven. Which range is usual, as the recipe and oven maker say?
options: About 200–230 °C
About 100–120 °C
About 140–150 °C
About 280–300 °C

questions.stem: Why does dough rise quickly in the first minutes in the oven (oven spring)?
options: Heat makes the gas grow before the yeast dies
The oven light pulls the dough upward
The crust sets first and then lifts the dough up
The salt melts and turns into gas

questions.stem: How can you check that a loaf is baked through?
options: It feels soft and doughy underneath
It sounds hollow when tapped underneath
It is still pale and shiny all over the top
It sticks to the tin when tipped out

questions.stem: A Jamaican spiced bun is often brushed with a glaze straight after baking. What is the glaze usually?
options: Cold water mixed with salt
Melted lard mixed with flour
Sugar syrup
Raw beaten egg white only

questions.stem: Which best describes Jamaican hard dough bread?
options: A flat bread cooked on a griddle with no yeast
A sweet cake with fruit and rum
A crisp, open loaf with large holes
A dense, close-textured, slightly sweet loaf

questions.stem: How is Jamaican coco bread usually shaped before baking?
options: Rolled into a long twisted plait
Pressed flat and cut into squares
Shaped into a round ball with a cross cut
Rolled flat and folded in half

questions.stem: Yeast doughnuts are fried in hot oil. What temperature is usual, as the recipe and fryer maker say?
options: About 100–120 °C
About 230–250 °C
About 170–190 °C
About 60–80 °C

questions.stem: Oil in a pan for doughnuts catches fire. What should you do?
options: Throw a jug of cold water on it straight away
Carry the burning pan outside quickly
Fan the flames out with a dry tea towel
Turn off the heat and use a fire blanket

questions.stem: Why are doughnuts lowered gently into the oil, away from you?
options: To keep the oil from losing its colour
So that the doughnuts sink straight to the bottom
So the sugar does not melt off them
To stop hot oil from splashing onto you

questions.stem: What makes croissant and Danish pastry dough different from plain bread dough?
options: It is deep-fried in oil
It is boiled in water first
It is layered with butter
It is steamed in a basket

questions.stem: Rolls topped with sesame seeds must be labelled. Why?
options: Sesame is a common allergen
Sesame makes the rolls more costly
Sesame seeds are a type of yeast
Sesame must be kept in the freezer

questions.stem: Which allergen is in almost every bread made from wheat flour?
options: Gluten
Peanut
Shellfish
Mustard

questions.stem: You have a small cut on your finger and are about to shape rolls. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as the oven will kill any germs
Wrap it in a paper towel and carry on working
Cover it with a blue plaster and wear a glove
Shape the rolls with your other hand only

questions.stem: Why is bread cooled on a wire rack after baking?
options: To make the crust go soft, damp and pale
So it can be put into bags while still hot
To stop the yeast from rising again
So the steam escapes and the base is dry

questions.stem: Where does plain bread go stale fastest?
options: In the fridge, at about 5 °C
In the freezer, well wrapped
In a clean bread bin
In a sealed bag on a shelf

questions.stem: Bread rolls will not be used for three days. What is the best way to keep them fresh?
options: Leave them uncovered on the counter
Keep them unwrapped in the fridge
Put them in the prover overnight
Wrap them well, label and freeze

questions.stem: Why should bread rolls for a hotel dinner be the same size and shape?
options: So they need less time in the oven
So guests will eat more butter
So the dough does not need proving
For a neat look and fair, costed portions

questions.stem: Why are some loaves cut (scored) on top with a sharp blade before baking?
options: To let the yeast out of the dough
To test whether the dough is cooked
To control where the loaf opens up
To stop the loaf from rising too much

questions.stem: How should dough be cleaned off the mixer bowl and hook?
options: Leave it to dry hard so it chips off later
Scrape it off, then wash, rinse and sanitise
Wipe it with a dry cloth and put it away
Rinse it in the sink with the raw meat trays

questions.stem: A bakery must have fresh rolls ready for a 7 a.m. breakfast. What should the baker do?
options: Start mixing at 6:55 a.m.
Plan each stage back from 7 a.m.
Bake yesterday's dough again
Use baking powder instead of yeast

questions.stem: Before working with food in a Jamaican bakery, what must a food handler get from the local health department?
options: A driver's licence
A Food Handler's Permit
A tax registration card
A trade licence for the shop

essays.stem: Explain what yeast needs to work, and how heat, salt and sugar affect it.
essays.modelAnswer: Yeast is a tiny living organism. To grow and make gas it needs food, which is sugar from the flour or added sugar, warmth, moisture from the water or milk, and time. As it feeds, it gives off carbon dioxide gas, which is trapped by the gluten and makes the dough rise, and a little alcohol, which adds flavour. This is called fermentation. Gentle warmth, from lukewarm liquid and a warm proving place, helps the yeast work faster. Cold slows it down, which is why dough can be kept in the fridge. Too much heat kills the yeast, so the liquid must never be hot, and the yeast dies when the bread is baked. Salt gives flavour and controls the yeast, but if it touches the yeast directly or too much is used, it slows or kills it. A little sugar feeds the yeast, but a lot of sugar slows it down.
markingPoints: Yeast needs food, warmth, moisture and time
It gives off carbon dioxide (and alcohol), which makes the dough rise
Warmth speeds it up, cold slows it down, too much heat kills it
Salt controls the yeast but slows or kills it in direct contact or in excess
A little sugar feeds it; a lot of sugar slows it

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to make a batch of bread rolls by the straight dough method, from weighing to baking.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands, put on clean uniform and cover my hair. I weigh strong flour, salt, sugar, yeast, fat and water accurately, keeping the salt away from the yeast. I mix everything together at once with lukewarm water to make a dough. I knead it by hand or with a dough hook until it is smooth and stretchy and passes the stretch test. I put it in a lightly oiled bowl, cover it and leave it in a warm place until it has doubled in size. I knock it back to press out the gas, then scale it into equal pieces, for example 60 g each, using the scales. I round each piece into a tight ball, shape it and place it on a lined tray with space between. I give it a final proof until a finger press springs back slowly, egg-wash it and bake it in a hot oven, as the recipe and oven maker say, until golden and hollow-sounding.
markingPoints: Hygiene and accurate weighing, with salt kept away from the yeast
Mixes all at once with lukewarm liquid and kneads until smooth and stretchy
First proof covered in a warm place until doubled
Knocks back, scales into equal pieces, rounds and shapes
Final proof, egg wash and bakes hot until golden and hollow-sounding

essays.stem: Explain why dough is kneaded, how to knead it by hand, and how to tell when it is ready.
essays.modelAnswer: Kneading develops the gluten, which is formed from the proteins in strong flour when they are mixed with water and worked. Good gluten is stretchy and strong, so it can trap the gas from the yeast and let the dough rise and hold its shape. Kneading also mixes the yeast evenly through the dough. To knead by hand, I put the dough on a clean, lightly floured surface. I push it away from me with the heel of my hand, fold it back over, turn it a quarter and push again, keeping a steady rhythm. I keep going for about ten minutes, or as the recipe says, without adding too much extra flour. At first the dough is rough and sticky. When it is ready it is smooth, soft and springy, and when I stretch a small piece it becomes thin enough to see light through without tearing.
markingPoints: Develops the gluten so the dough can trap gas and hold its shape
Mixes the yeast evenly
Correct hand method: push with the heel, fold, turn, repeat
Uses a clean surface and not too much extra flour
Ready when smooth and springy and a piece stretches thin without tearing

essays.stem: Explain the first proof and the final proof of a yeast dough: what happens, the right conditions, and how to tell when the dough is ready.
essays.modelAnswer: After kneading, the dough has its first proof, also called bulk fermentation. The yeast feeds and gives off gas, so the dough rises, and flavour develops. The dough is put in a lightly oiled bowl, covered so it does not form a skin, and left in a warm place free from draughts until it has about doubled in size. It is then knocked back, scaled and shaped. The final proof happens after shaping. The shaped pieces are put on trays or in tins, covered, and left in a warm, moist place, often a prover set as the maker says, so they rise again before baking. The dough is ready when it has grown to about the right size and a gentle finger press leaves a dent that springs back slowly. If it springs back fast it needs longer; if it does not spring back it is over-proved.
markingPoints: First proof: yeast makes gas, dough rises, flavour develops
Covered, in a warm place without draughts, until about doubled
Final proof after shaping, in a warm, moist place or prover
Ready when a finger press springs back slowly
Explains under-proved (springs back fast) and over-proved (no spring)

essays.stem: Describe how to make Jamaican coco bread.
essays.modelAnswer: I weigh strong flour, salt, sugar and yeast, keeping the salt away from the yeast. I warm coconut milk until it is lukewarm and melt some butter. I mix the flour, sugar, yeast and salt with the coconut milk and butter to make a soft dough, and knead it until it is smooth and stretchy. I cover it and leave it in a warm place until it has doubled in size. I knock it back and scale it into equal pieces, then round each one. I roll each piece into a flat oval or round, brush the top with melted butter and fold it in half, so it can be opened later for a patty. I place them on a lined tray, cover them and give them a final proof. I bake them at the heat the recipe and oven maker say until lightly golden, then brush them with butter so they stay soft. I label the allergens: wheat and milk.
markingPoints: Weighs ingredients with coconut milk and butter, salt apart from the yeast
Makes and kneads a soft, smooth dough
First proof, knock back, scale and round
Rolls flat, brushes with butter and folds in half
Final proof, bakes until lightly golden, brushes with butter and labels allergens

essays.stem: Describe three faults in bread or rolls, the likely cause of each, and how to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Bread that is small, heavy and tight was often under-proved, or the yeast was killed by liquid that was too hot, or the dough was not kneaded enough. I prevent this by using lukewarm liquid, kneading until the dough passes the stretch test and proving until a finger press springs back slowly. Bread that has collapsed, has large holes and tastes sour or yeasty was over-proved. I check the dough often during proving and bake it as soon as it is ready. Bread with a pale, soft crust was baked in an oven that was too cool, was not baked long enough or had too little sugar. I preheat the oven to the heat the recipe and oven maker say and bake until it is golden and sounds hollow. A hard skin on the dough means it was not covered while proving, so I always cover it.
markingPoints: First fault with a correct cause
Correct prevention for the first fault
Second fault with a correct cause and prevention
Third fault with a correct cause and prevention
Uses correct terms (proving, kneading, oven heat, skin)

essays.stem: Describe how to fry yeast doughnuts safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the deep fryer is clean, in good order and filled with fresh oil to the line the maker shows, never above it. I heat the oil to the temperature the recipe and fryer maker say, often about 170–190 °C, using the thermostat or a thermometer. I keep the area dry and make sure a fire blanket and a suitable extinguisher are close by. I lift the proved doughnuts carefully on a slice or on squares of paper and lower them gently into the oil, away from me, so the oil does not splash. I do not overcrowd the fryer, because the oil will cool and the doughnuts will be greasy. I turn them once with a slotted spoon when the first side is golden. I lift them out, drain them on kitchen paper and toss them in sugar or fill them when cool. I never leave hot oil unattended or put water near it, and if oil catches fire I turn off the heat and use the fire blanket.
markingPoints: Checks the fryer and fills oil only to the maker's line
Heats oil to the temperature the recipe and fryer maker say
Lowers doughnuts gently away from the body and does not overcrowd
Turns, drains and finishes them correctly
Fire safety: blanket nearby, never water, never leave hot oil unattended

essays.stem: Explain what an enriched dough is, how it is handled and baked differently from a plain dough, and give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: An enriched dough has extra ingredients such as butter, milk, coconut milk, sugar, eggs, spices or dried fruit added to the basic flour, yeast, salt and water. These make the bread softer, richer and sweeter, and help it keep longer. Examples are coco bread, cinnamon rolls, sweet buns, brioche and a yeast-raised Jamaican spiced bun. Because fat and sugar slow the yeast, enriched doughs often need more yeast or a longer proof. The fat may be added after some kneading so the gluten can form first. The dough is softer and stickier, so it needs gentle handling. Because of the sugar, milk and eggs, the crust browns faster, so enriched doughs are often baked at a lower heat than plain bread, as the recipe and oven maker say, and may be covered if they brown too soon. They are often glazed with egg wash or sugar syrup.
markingPoints: Definition: extra fat, milk, sugar, eggs, spices or fruit added
Softer, richer, sweeter and keeps longer
Suitable examples (for example coco bread, cinnamon rolls, bun)
Fat and sugar slow the yeast, so more yeast or longer proving may be needed
Browns faster, so baked at a lower heat; often glazed

essays.stem: Explain how a baker plans the timing of a batch of yeast goods so that they are fresh for service.
essays.modelAnswer: The baker starts from the time the bread must be ready, for example 7 a.m. for breakfast, and works backwards through every stage. Cooling may take about 30 minutes, baking 15 to 20 minutes for rolls, the final proof 30 to 60 minutes, shaping 20 minutes, the first proof about an hour, and mixing and kneading 15 minutes, or as the recipe says. Adding these up tells the baker when to start, with a little spare time. The baker checks that the ingredients are in stock and that the mixer, prover and oven are free and working. The oven is switched on in time to be hot when the dough is ready. Doughs can be slowed in the fridge overnight, so they are ready to shape and bake early in the morning. The baker writes the plan on a production sheet and checks the dough at each stage, because warm weather in Jamaica can make dough prove faster.
markingPoints: Works backwards from the time the bread is needed
Allows time for each stage (mix, proofs, shape, bake, cool)
Checks ingredients and equipment and preheats the oven in time
Uses the fridge to slow dough where needed
Writes a production plan and checks the dough, allowing for warm weather

essays.stem: Explain how to cool, store, label and present bread and other yeast goods so that they are safe and fresh.
essays.modelAnswer: I cool bread on a wire rack so the steam escapes and the crust and base do not go soggy. I do not wrap it until it is completely cool, or it will sweat and go mouldy. Bread for the same day is kept covered or in a clean bread bin in a cool, dry place, away from pests. Bread is not kept in the fridge, because it goes stale faster there. Bread for later is wrapped well, labelled and frozen. Yeast goods with cream or custard fillings are kept covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. Every item is labelled with its name, the date made and its allergens, such as wheat, milk, eggs and sesame, and stock is used first in, first out. For service I present rolls of the same size in clean baskets or on trays, handled with tongs or gloves.
markingPoints: Cools on a wire rack and wraps only when completely cool
Stores covered in a cool, dry place; not in the fridge; freezes for later
Keeps cream or custard-filled items in the fridge at 5 °C or below (or as the plan says)
Labels with name, date and allergens and rotates stock
Presents same-sized items cleanly, handled with tongs or gloves

practical1.title: Make a straight dough and produce bread rolls in three shapes
practical1.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipe, list the allergens and set up. Each member makes their own straight dough from about 500 g of strong flour: weigh the ingredients (keeping the salt away from the yeast), mix with lukewarm water, knead by hand until the dough passes the stretch test, and give it a first proof, covered, in a warm place. Then each member knocks back the dough, scales it into equal pieces of the weight the assessor gives (for example 60 g), rounds them and shapes them into three shapes: plain rounds, knots and small plaits. Give a final proof, test it with a finger press, egg-wash and bake at the heat the recipe and oven maker say. Each member tests their rolls for doneness, cools them on a wire rack and weighs three to check they are even. Label with name, date and allergens, and clean down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Strong flour, salt, sugar, yeast, butter or shortening, an egg for egg wash, sesame or other seeds (optional) and water
Scales, bowls, a measuring jug, a dough scraper, a pastry brush and a thermometer for the water
Lined baking trays, cling film or clean cloths to cover the dough, and a wire rack
A prover or a warm place for proving, and an oven
Dry oven gloves, labels and pens, and cleaning materials
photos: The group in clean uniform with the work area set up and allergens listed
Ingredients weighed, with the salt and yeast kept apart
A member kneading by hand, and the stretch test on the dough
The dough covered for its first proof, then doubled in size
Dough scaled into equal pieces on the scales
The three shapes on the tray after the final proof
Baked rolls cooling on the wire rack
Rolls labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Weighed the ingredients accurately and kept the salt away from the yeast
Used lukewarm liquid and kneaded until the dough passed the stretch test
Proved the dough covered in a warm place until doubled
Knocked back and scaled pieces to the correct weight
Shaped neat, even rounds, knots and plaits
Tested the final proof and baked the rolls until golden and hollow-sounding
Cooled the rolls on a rack, labelled them and cleaned the area and equipment
safety: If a mixer is used, keep the guard on and switch off before touching the dough or hook
Use dry oven gloves for hot trays and tell others when you are carrying something hot
Wipe up flour and spills at once so nobody slips
Cover any cut with a blue plaster and a glove

practical2.title: Produce Jamaican hard dough bread loaves and coco bread
practical2.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipes, list the allergens and set up. Each member makes their own hard dough bread dough for one loaf: weigh, mix, knead until smooth and firm, prove covered, knock back, shape and place in a greased loaf tin, and give a final proof. The group also makes one batch of coco bread dough with lukewarm coconut milk and butter, with each member doing a named stage (weighing, mixing, kneading, checking the proof). Each member then scales and shapes at least two coco breads: roll flat, brush with butter and fold in half. Bake the loaves and the coco bread at the heat the recipe and oven maker say. Each member tests their own loaf for doneness by tapping underneath, with the assessor watching, and cools it on a wire rack. Brush the coco bread with butter, slice one loaf to show the crumb, label everything with name, date and allergens, and clean down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Strong flour, sugar, salt, yeast, shortening or butter and water for the hard dough bread
Coconut milk, butter, sugar, salt, yeast and strong flour for the coco bread
Scales, bowls, a measuring jug, dough scrapers, rolling pins, pastry brushes and a bread knife
Greased loaf tins, lined baking trays, cling film or clean cloths, and a wire rack
A mixer with a dough hook and guard (if used), a prover or warm place, and an oven
Dry oven gloves, labels and pens, and cleaning materials
photos: The group in clean uniform with the work area set up and allergens listed
Each member's hard dough bread dough after kneading
Loaves shaped in their tins before the final proof
Coco bread rolled flat, buttered and folded
The finger-press test on the proved dough
A member tapping a baked loaf underneath
A sliced loaf showing the close crumb, and the finished coco bread
Products labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Weighed the ingredients accurately, kept the salt away from the yeast and used lukewarm liquid
Kneaded the dough until smooth and well developed
Proved the dough correctly, covered, and tested the final proof
Shaped a neat loaf in the tin and folded the coco bread evenly
Baked to the correct colour and tested the loaf by tapping underneath
Cooled on a rack and sliced only when cool, with a sharp bread knife used safely
Labelled the products and cleaned the area and equipment
safety: Keep the mixer guard on and switch off and wait for the hook to stop before touching the dough
Use dry oven gloves for hot tins and turn loaves out on a board away from your body
Use the bread knife with a sawing action, fingers clear, on a board that does not slip
Wipe up spills at once so nobody slips
